newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end down as selling pressure weighs.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end down as selling pressure weighs.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed lower on Monday as selling pressures weighed on the market following gains seen last week.
The Treasury announced it would scrap sales of conventional 10-year notes in July and October. It introduced a new five-year inflation-protected security.

A lower federal budget deficit and the success of the inflation-indexed securities that the Treasury began to sell last January had allowed the Treasury to eliminate two of six annual sales of fixed-rate 10-year notes, a spokesman said.
"This was the hallmark of a downtrending day. We may see new lows on Tuesday," said Chris Rupkey, economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.
Rupkey said that after hitting a low on Tuesday, the long end of the curve could stage a comeback ahead of retail sales data on Thursday.
"It's always (Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan) Greenspan's peragotive to turn things around 180 degrees," Rupkey said. Greenspan was scheduled to speak on Tuesday night in New York.
Traders said heavy corporate supply and asset-backed securities issuance helped to contribute to weakness in the Treasuries market on Monday.

"Supply may be the most visable factor people are pointing their fingers to, but we see this kind of supply fairly often," said Anthony Karadakis, senior financial economist at First National Bank of Chicago.

There was a heavy calendar of investment-grade and high-yield corparate bond issuance this week as many companies sought to lock in what are perceived as low interest rates before obvious signs of inflation surfaced and interest rates rose.

Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp., said the decline in the value of the dollar also was taking a toll on bond prices. Talk that Germany may not qualify for European Monetary Union status on deadline pushed the mark higher against the dollar.
Stephansen said there also was a breather from Friday's rally, which she said in many repsects was difficult to understand.
"What had been viewed as a slowdown (in May nonfarm payrolls) was wiped out by the upward revision in April," Stephansen said.
Karadakis said many players entered the week with a defensive posture and low volume could be exaggerating price movement.
He said there was a clear calendar in the first three days of this week before retail sales on Thursday and activity was likely to remain contained.
"Some reports could provide the market (with the incentive) to do something, but it looks like a somewhat less than an even bet the economy is slowing," Karadakis said.
"The slowdown (should it occur in the second quarter) may not prove to be sustainable, but could give them (the Federal Reserve) a bit more time to wait," he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 97-13/32, down 20/32, yielding 6.83 percent.

Two-year notes ended at 100-6/32, down 3/32 to yield 6.15 percent. Five-year notes fell 8/32 to 100-9/32 to yield 6.43 percent and the 10-year note was off 13/32 to 100-18/32, its yield at 6.55 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell one basis point to 4.91 percent, six-month rates rose one basis point to 5.18 percent and year bill rates rose four basis points to 5.42 percent.
